content: The term Matthew Effect originates from a line spoken by the Master in Jesus' parable of the talents, as described in the Gospel of Matthew. In the sociology of science, the Matthew Effect was introduced by Robert K. Merton to describe a phenomenon where renowned scientists often receive more recognition than lesser-known researchers, even when their contributions are similar. This effect also implies that credit is disproportionately given to already famous researchers. For instance, in collaborative projects, prestigious awards or prizes are frequently granted to the most senior researcher, even if the majority of the work was carried out by a graduate student. Specific examples of the Matthew Effect in science include the case of John von Neumann, a 20th-century mathematician often referred to as the father of game theory or the father of the computer. However, some of his influential publications were restatements of ideas developed by his collaborators, such as in the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. Another example involves the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physics, where George Sudarshan was controversially excluded from recognition for his contributions to the Sudarshan-Glauber representation in quantum optics. Instead, Roy J. Glauber received the prize for the same work. Critics have pointed out that the Nobel Committee, constrained by Alfred Nobel's will to limit the number of recipients to three per year, has often overlooked scientists who made foundational contributions to a topic while awarding the prize to others working in the same field. In mathematics, the Matthew Effect is evident in cases where a concept originally developed by one mathematician is later attributed to a more famous mathematician who worked on it at a later time. These instances are well-documented and highlight the tendency to associate credit with fame rather than originality. The Matilda Effect is a related concept that highlights the systematic neglect of women's contributions to science. Named after early feminist Matilda Joslyn Gage, the term was introduced by historian of science Margaret Rossiter in 1993. The Matilda Effect underscores the gender bias in recognizing scientific achievements, where the work of women is often overlooked or attributed to their male counterparts. In the field of education, the term Matthew Effect has been applied by psychologist Keith Stanovich to describe a phenomenon observed in the development of reading skills. Early success in learning to read often leads to continued success, while failure to acquire reading skills by the third or fourth year of schooling can result in lifelong difficulties in learning new skills. Children who struggle with reading tend to read less, which widens the gap between them and their peers. As students progress to stages where they must read to learn, their reading difficulties hinder their ability to succeed in other subjects, causing them to fall further behind. This often leads to higher dropout rates and limits their ability to use education as a means of improving their lives, perpetuating a cycle of disadvantage. Keith Stanovich explains that slow reading acquisition has cognitive, behavioral, and motivational consequences that impede the development of other cognitive skills and academic performance. As reading skills develop, they influence and are influenced by other cognitive processes. When reading development is delayed, it inhibits the growth of knowledge bases that are interdependent with reading. Over time, these deficits become more generalized, affecting broader areas of cognition and behavior. As one struggling nine-year-old poignantly put it, Reading affects everything you do.
